questions.question: What is the Java Collections Framework hierarchy?
questions.title: Java Collections Framework Hierarchy Explained
questions.direct_answer: **Iterable** is the root interface; **Collection** extends it and branches into **List**, **Set**, and **Queue**. **Map** is a separate hierarchy — it does NOT extend Collection because it stores key-value pairs, not single elements. Concrete classes like `ArrayList`, `HashSet`, and `HashMap` implement these interfaces.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can draw the framework's backbone from memory and correctly place Map outside the Collection branch
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Drawing Map as a child of Collection, or forgetting Queue is a third branch alongside List and Set
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the for-each loop works because Iterable sits at the root, and that Map bridges back via keySet/values/entrySet views

sections.title: The Collections Framework Hierarchy
sections.content:
The **Java Collections Framework** is a set of interfaces and classes for storing and processing groups of objects. It is built on a clean tree that starts with **Iterable** at the very top — the interface that gives you the ability to loop with a for-each. **Collection** extends `Iterable` and adds the core group operations: `add`, `remove`, `size`, `contains`.

From `Collection`, three branches grow: **List** (ordered, allows duplicates), **Set** (no duplicates), and **Queue** (holds elements before processing). The key design decision every interviewer probes: **Map** does NOT extend `Collection`. A `Map` stores **key-value pairs**, so forcing it under `Collection`'s single-element contract would produce a confusing API. Think of a phonebook (Map: name to number) versus a shopping list (List: just items) — different shapes of data.

sections.title: The Hierarchy at a Glance
sections.content:
violet|Iterable|~Root of the tree|the single method iterator()|enables for-each|in java.lang, not java.util
blue|Collection|~Extends Iterable|add, remove, size, contains|parent of List/Set/Queue|the group contract
emerald|List / Set / Queue|~Three Collection branches|List: ordered, duplicates ok|Set: unique elements|Queue: FIFO / priority
amber|Map|~Separate hierarchy|stores key-value pairs|does NOT extend Collection|HashMap, TreeMap, LinkedHashMap
cyan|Concrete classes|~The implementations|ArrayList, LinkedList|HashSet, TreeSet|HashMap, LinkedHashMap

sections.title: The Hierarchy in Code
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying Map extends Collection.** This is the single most-tested misconception. Map is a sibling hierarchy, not a child — its `put(key, value)` cannot fit `Collection.add(element)`.
- **Forgetting Queue.** Many freshers list only List and Set. Queue (and Deque) is the third branch, with `LinkedList` and `PriorityQueue` as implementations.
- **Confusing Collection with Collections.** `Collection` (singular) is the interface; `Collections` (plural) is a utility class of static helpers like `sort` and `unmodifiableList`.
- **Putting Iterable in java.util.** `Iterable` actually lives in `java.lang`; everything below it lives in `java.util`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Iterable** — the root in `java.lang`; one method `iterator()`, enables for-each.
- **Collection** — extends Iterable; adds `add`, `remove`, `size`, `contains`.
- **List / Set / Queue** — the three Collection branches: ordered+duplicates, unique, FIFO.
- **Map is separate** — stores key-value pairs, does NOT extend Collection.
- **Map bridges back** — `keySet()`, `values()`, `entrySet()` expose Collection views.
- **Program to the interface** — declare `List`/`Set`/`Map`, instantiate `ArrayList`/`HashSet`/`HashMap`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The Java Collections Framework is a set of interfaces and classes for storing groups of objects, and it sits on a clean tree. At the very top is Iterable — that's the simplest interface, it just gives you an iterator so you can loop over things with a for-each. Collection extends Iterable and adds the core operations like add, remove, size, and contains. From Collection you get three branches. The first is List, which keeps elements in order and allows duplicates — that's ArrayList and LinkedList. The second is Set, which doesn't allow duplicates — that's HashSet and TreeSet. The third is Queue, for elements you process in sequence — like LinkedList or PriorityQueue. Now the part interviewers love to test: Map is completely separate. It does not extend Collection. The reason is that Map stores key-value pairs, and its methods like put and get take two arguments, which simply don't fit Collection's single-element contract built around add. If Map were forced under Collection, the API would be confusing. Map does give you a bridge, though — you can call keySet to get the keys as a Set, values to get the values as a Collection, and entrySet to get the pairs. So the mental picture is: Iterable at the top, then Collection splitting into List, Set, and Queue, with Map standing on its own beside them. The classic mistake is saying Map extends Collection — it's a sibling, not a child.

questions.question: Why is Map not part of the Collection interface in Java?
questions.title: Why Map Does Not Extend Collection in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Map** stores **key-value pairs** and its core methods — `put(K,V)`, `get(K)` — work on two-part entries, which is incompatible with **Collection**'s single-element contract (`add(E)`, `remove(Object)`). Making Map extend Collection would force a meaningless `add(element)` signature, so Java keeps them as **separate hierarchies** and bridges them with `keySet`, `values`, and `entrySet` views.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand interface-contract design rather than just memorizing 'Map is different'
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Answering 'they're just different types' without explaining why add(E) cannot express put(K,V)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Collection views (keySet/values/entrySet) that let you still treat a Map's parts as collections

sections.title: The Contract Mismatch
sections.content:
Map staying out of the `Collection` hierarchy is not arbitrary — it follows directly from **interface contract design**. `Collection` is built around **single elements**: `add(E element)`, `remove(Object o)`, `contains(Object o)`. Every method takes one item.

`Map` is built around **key-value pairs**: `put(K key, V value)`, `get(Object key)`, `containsKey(Object key)`. If `Map` extended `Collection`, what would `add(E element)` mean — add a key? a value? a pair? There is no clean answer with one parameter. Forcing it would also break the idea that you can use a `Map` wherever a `Collection` is expected. So Java keeps them separate, and provides **Collection views** — `keySet()`, `values()`, `entrySet()` — so you can still treat a Map's parts as collections when you need to.

sections.title: Two Contracts, One Bridge
sections.content:
blue|Collection contract|~Single elements|add(E element)|remove(Object o)|contains(Object o)
amber|Map contract|~Key-value pairs|put(K key, V value)|get(Object key)|containsKey(Object key)
emerald|The clash|~Why add() can't fit|add takes ONE argument|a pair needs TWO|no sensible single-arg form
cyan|The bridge|~Collection views|keySet() returns a Set|values() returns a Collection|entrySet() returns Set of entries

sections.title: Why the single-argument contract breaks down for a pair
Map keeps its own contract, and bridges back with views
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Surface answer.** Saying only 'Map is for pairs, Collection is for elements' misses the point — explain that `add(E)` cannot encode two values.
- **Forgetting the views.** A strong answer mentions `keySet`, `values`, and `entrySet` as the bridge between the hierarchies.
- **Calling it a Java quirk.** It's deliberate API design; mixing the contracts would pollute both interfaces with ambiguous methods.
- **Thinking you can't iterate a Map.** You can — via `entrySet()` in a for-each loop.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Collection** = single-element contract: `add`, `remove`, `contains`.
- **Map** = key-value contract: `put`, `get`, `containsKey`.
- `add(E element)` cannot express `put(K key, V value)` — that's why no inheritance.
- Map provides **Collection views**: `keySet` (Set), `values` (Collection), `entrySet` (Set of entries).
- Views are **live** — mutating them updates the backing map.
- Iterate a Map by looping over `entrySet()`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Map doesn't extend Collection because their contracts are fundamentally incompatible. Collection is designed around single elements. When you call add, you pass one thing; when you call remove or contains, you work with one element. But Map is designed around key-value pairs. When you call put, you pass two things — a key and a value. So if Map extended Collection, what would the add method even mean? You'd somehow need to pass both a key and a value into a method that only takes one parameter, and that doesn't work. It's not just inconvenient, it's bad interface design — you couldn't substitute a Map anywhere a Collection is expected without breaking the contract. That's why Java keeps them as two separate hierarchies. But here's the clever part: Map gives you Collection views. You call keySet and get back a Set of all the keys. You call values and get a Collection of all the values. And you call entrySet to get a Set of key-value entries, which is exactly how you loop over a Map with a for-each. Those views are live, so if you remove a key from the keySet, it disappears from the map too. The common mistake is just saying Map and Collection are different without explaining why the signatures clash. The real insight is that add of one element and put of a key and value are simply incompatible contracts, and that's the whole reason they live in separate trees.

questions.question: What is the difference between Collection and Collections in Java?
questions.title: Collection vs Collections in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Collection** (singular) is an **interface** — the root of the collection hierarchy defining `add`, `remove`, `size`. **Collections** (plural) is a **utility class** in `java.util` containing only **static helper methods** like `sort`, `shuffle`, `unmodifiableList`, and `synchronizedList`. There is no inheritance relationship between them — one is a contract, the other is a toolbox.

interviewer_intent.testing: Attention to detail and familiarity with standard-library naming conventions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Collections as a variable type, or claiming Collections extends/implements Collection
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note the same naming pattern recurs with Array vs Arrays, and show a real Collections.sort / unmodifiableList call

sections.title: Two Different Roles, One Letter Apart
sections.content:
This is a naming trap. **Collection** (singular) is an **interface** in `java.util` — the parent of `List`, `Set`, and `Queue` — defining the core contract: `add`, `remove`, `size`, `isEmpty`, `iterator`. You implement it (indirectly) when you use `ArrayList`, `HashSet`, etc.

**Collections** (plural) is a **final utility class**, also in `java.util`, that holds only **static methods** — like the `Math` class. You never instantiate it; you call helpers such as `Collections.sort`, `Collections.unmodifiableList`, `Collections.synchronizedList`, and `Collections.shuffle`. They sound nearly identical, but one is a *contract* and the other is a *toolbox*.

sections.title: Collection vs Collections
sections.content:
| Aspect | Collection | Collections |
|---|---|---|
| **Type** | Interface | Utility (final) class |
| **Purpose** | Defines the group contract | Provides static helper methods |
| **Used as** | A variable / parameter type | Called as `Collections.method(...)` |
| **Instantiate?** | No (it's an interface) | No (private constructor) |
| **Examples** | `add`, `remove`, `size`, `contains` | `sort`, `shuffle`, `max`, `unmodifiableList` |

sections.title: Contract vs Toolbox
sections.content:
blue|Collection (singular)|~The interface|root of List/Set/Queue|defines add, remove, size|use it as a type
emerald|Collections (plural)|~The utility class|only static methods|sort, shuffle, max, min|private constructor
amber|No relationship|~Names look alike|no inheritance link|one is a contract|the other is helpers
cyan|Same pattern|~Recurs in the JDK|Array vs Arrays|Object vs Objects|plural = static helpers

sections.title: The mistake: treating Collections as a type
The fix: Collection as the type, Collections for the helpers
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use **Collection** as a **declared type** for variables, parameters, and return types when you want to accept any group implementation: `void process(Collection<Order> orders)` accepts a List, Set, or Queue.

Reach for **Collections** when you need to **operate on** a collection: `Collections.sort` before display, `Collections.unmodifiableList` when returning internal state so callers can't mutate it, `Collections.synchronizedList` for simple thread-safe wrapping, and `Collections.emptyList` to return a safe empty result instead of `null`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Collection** = interface (the contract); **Collections** = utility class (the helpers).
- **No inheritance** between them — totally unrelated despite the names.
- Common `Collections` methods: `sort`, `reverse`, `shuffle`, `binarySearch`, `max`, `min`, `unmodifiableList`.
- `Collections.unmodifiableList` returns a **read-only view**; mutating it throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.
- Same pattern elsewhere: **Array vs Arrays**, **Object vs Objects**.
- Use `Collection` as a type; call `Collections.` for operations.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Collection and Collections are two completely different things with confusingly similar names. Collection, singular, is an interface. It's the parent of List, Set, and Queue, and it defines methods like add, remove, size, and isEmpty. When you write Collection as a variable type, you're using this interface. Collections, plural with an s, is a utility class. It's like the Math class — you never create an instance of it, you just call its static methods. For example, Collections dot sort will sort a list for you, Collections dot unmodifiableList wraps a list so it can't be modified, and Collections dot shuffle randomizes the order. There's no inheritance relationship between them at all; Collections doesn't extend or implement Collection. They just have similar names because one is a toolbox for working with the other. A common mistake freshers make is writing Collections as a type, like Collections of String — that doesn't compile, because the interface is Collection, singular. Another mistake is not knowing the utility methods exist and writing manual loops to sort or find the maximum, when Collections dot sort and Collections dot max already do it. A nice detail to mention is that Java uses this same naming pattern elsewhere — Array versus Arrays, and Object versus Objects — where the plural version is always the static helper class. Recognizing that pattern helps you find utility methods quickly.

questions.question: Why are List, Set, and Map interfaces rather than concrete classes?
questions.title: Why List, Set, Map Are Interfaces in Java
questions.direct_answer: They are interfaces so you can **program to an abstraction, not an implementation**: your code depends only on the contract, so you can swap `ArrayList` for `LinkedList` (or `HashMap` for `LinkedHashMap`) by changing one line at construction. This decoupling is the **Liskov Substitution Principle** in action and adds zero runtime cost.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of interface-based design, decoupling, and polymorphism — not just reciting 'flexibility'
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying interfaces are 'faster', or giving vague answers like 'for flexibility' with no concrete reasoning
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show that declaring the field/parameter as List lets you swap the implementation in one place while all callers stay unchanged

sections.title: Program to Abstractions
sections.content:
Making `List`, `Set`, and `Map` **interfaces** rather than concrete classes is a deliberate design choice rooted in one principle: **program to an interface, not an implementation**. When you declare `List<Order> orders` instead of `ArrayList<Order> orders`, your code depends only on the *contract* — the methods `List` promises — not on how `ArrayList` resizes its internal array.

That means you can swap `ArrayList` for `LinkedList`, or `HashMap` for `LinkedHashMap`, without touching a single caller. This is **decoupling**, and it's the **Liskov Substitution Principle**: any implementation can substitute for the interface. Requirements change — today you need random access (`ArrayList`), tomorrow fast insertion at the ends (`LinkedList`) — and interface-based design lets you adapt by editing only the construction line.

sections.title: Interface vs Concrete Declaration
sections.content:
rose|Concrete type|~ArrayList everywhere|callers coupled to ArrayList|swap = edit many files|leaks implementation detail
emerald|Interface type|~List everywhere|callers depend on contract|swap = edit one line|hides implementation
blue|Why it works|~Polymorphism|JVM dispatches to real type|no runtime overhead|Liskov Substitution
amber|Daily rule|~Declare abstract, build concrete|field/param/return: List|construction: new ArrayList|tests can inject fakes

sections.title: Coupled to the concrete class — callers are locked in
Depend on the interface — swap freely
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Concrete types in signatures.** `ArrayList<Order>` as a parameter blocks callers from passing a `LinkedList`. Use `List<Order>`.
- **Believing interfaces are slower.** There is no overhead — the JVM dispatches directly to the real implementation's methods.
- **Choosing concrete because it 'feels simpler'.** The interface is clearer: it tells callers what operations exist without exposing internals like array resizing.
- **Forgetting return types.** Returning `ArrayList` leaks the implementation; return `List` to reserve the right to change.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Program to the interface** — `List`/`Set`/`Map`, not `ArrayList`/`HashSet`/`HashMap`.
- **Decoupling** — callers depend on the contract, not on internals.
- **Liskov Substitution** — any implementation can stand in for the interface.
- **One-line swap** — change the construction site, callers untouched.
- **Parameters & return types** — accept and return interfaces for maximum flexibility.
- **Zero overhead** — interface dispatch costs nothing at runtime.
- Declare abstract, **instantiate concrete** at one point.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: They're interfaces because of a core design principle: program to an interface, not an implementation. When you declare a variable as List instead of ArrayList, your code only depends on the contract — the methods List defines — and it doesn't care whether the implementation uses an array, a linked structure, or something else. That's called decoupling. Why does it matter? Because requirements change. Today you might use ArrayList because you need fast random access by index. Tomorrow you realize you're doing lots of insertions at the front, so you switch to LinkedList. If you programmed to the List interface, you change exactly one line — where you construct the object — and every caller keeps working. That's the Liskov Substitution Principle: any List implementation can substitute for another. If instead you'd declared everything as ArrayList, you'd have to change method signatures, casts, and caller code all over the place. The same logic applies to method parameters: if your method takes ArrayList, callers can only pass ArrayList, but if it takes List, they can pass any implementation. A common mistake is thinking interfaces are slower or add overhead — they don't, the JVM dispatches straight to the real method on ArrayList or LinkedList. Another mistake is saying interfaces give flexibility without explaining why. The concrete reason is that you can change the implementation in a single place without touching any client code, and that's what keeps large codebases maintainable and testable.

questions.question: What is the Iterable interface and why is it at the top of the hierarchy?
questions.title: Iterable Interface in Java Collections
questions.direct_answer: **Iterable** has a single method, `iterator()`, that returns an **Iterator**. It sits at the top because it defines the minimum contract needed for a **for-each loop** — the compiler rewrites for-each into `iterator()`, `hasNext()`, `next()` calls. Every `Collection` is `Iterable`, but a custom class can be `Iterable` without being a full Collection.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why for-each works and the difference between Iterable and Iterator
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Iterable (the factory) with Iterator (the cursor), or thinking for-each only works on arrays/collections
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a custom class implementing Iterable to get for-each support without implementing the whole Collection contract

sections.title: The Minimalist Root
sections.content:
**Iterable** (in `java.lang`) is the simplest possible contract for 'something you can loop over'. It has exactly one method: `iterator()`, which returns an **Iterator**. The `Iterator` then drives the loop with `hasNext()` (are there more elements?), `next()` (give me the next one), and optionally `remove()`.

Iterable is at the top because it is the **minimum requirement** for a for-each loop. When you write `for (String s : items)`, the compiler quietly rewrites it into calls to `iterator()`, `hasNext()`, and `next()`. `Collection` extends `Iterable` so every List, Set, and Queue is loopable. The key insight: **not every Iterable needs to be a Collection** — a read-only sequence, a lazy generator, or a database cursor can implement just `Iterable` and gain for-each support without `add`/`remove`/`size`.

sections.title: Iterable vs Iterator
sections.content:
violet|Iterable|~The factory|one method: iterator()|lives in java.lang|root of the hierarchy
blue|Iterator|~The cursor|hasNext(), next(), remove()|produced by iterator()|holds the loop position
emerald|for-each|~Compiler sugar|rewritten to iterator/hasNext/next|works on any Iterable|also works on arrays (special case)
amber|Minimal contract|~Why it's the root|no add/remove/size required|lazy sequences can implement it|Collection extends it

sections.title: A Custom Iterable Without Being a Collection
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Iterable vs Iterator confusion.** `Iterable` is the factory (`iterator()`); `Iterator` is the cursor (`hasNext`/`next`). You implement Iterable; it hands back an Iterator.
- **Thinking for-each is only for arrays/collections.** Any class implementing `Iterable` gets for-each for free.
- **Implementing Collection when Iterable is enough.** A read-only sequence forced to implement Collection must throw `UnsupportedOperationException` from `add`/`remove` — just implement Iterable instead.
- **Forgetting arrays are a special case.** Arrays support for-each via a compiler rule, not by being Iterable.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Iterable** — one method, `iterator()`; the minimum contract for for-each.
- **Iterator** — `hasNext()`, `next()`, optional `remove()`; performs the iteration.
- The compiler rewrites **for-each** into iterator/hasNext/next calls.
- **Collection extends Iterable** — all collections are iterable; not all iterables are collections.
- A custom class can implement **Iterable** for for-each without full Collection support.
- Enables **lazy sequences** that generate elements on demand.
- `Iterable` lives in `java.lang`, not `java.util`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Iterable is the root interface of the collections hierarchy, and it's incredibly simple. It has just one method, iterator, which returns an Iterator object. That Iterator has three methods: hasNext to check if there are more elements, next to get the next element, and remove to optionally delete the current one. Iterable sits at the top because it defines the absolute minimum contract for something that can be looped over. When you write a for-each loop, the compiler quietly translates it into calls to iterator, hasNext, and next behind the scenes — that's literally all a for-each needs. Collection extends Iterable, which is why every List, Set, or Queue can be looped over. But here's the key design insight: not every Iterable needs to be a Collection. You might have a custom class that generates values on demand, or wraps a database cursor, or fetches data from an API page by page. Those things can be looped over, so they should implement Iterable — but they don't support add, remove, or size. If they were forced to implement the full Collection contract, they'd have to throw exceptions from all those methods. Iterable lets them express exactly what they need: the ability to iterate. A common point of confusion is mixing up Iterable and Iterator. Iterable is the factory — it produces an Iterator. The Iterator is the cursor that actually walks through the elements and remembers where you are. So you implement Iterable on your class, and its iterator method returns a fresh Iterator each time.

questions.question: What are the key implementations for List, Set, and Map in Java?
questions.title: Key Java Collections Implementations: List, Set, Map
questions.direct_answer: **List**: `ArrayList` (resizable array, fast random access) and `LinkedList` (doubly linked, fast at the ends). **Set**: `HashSet` (unordered, O(1)), `LinkedHashSet` (insertion order), `TreeSet` (sorted, O(log n)). **Map**: `HashMap` (unordered, O(1)), `LinkedHashMap` (insertion/access order), `TreeMap` (sorted by key, O(log n)).

interviewer_intent.testing: Breadth across all three sub-hierarchies and awareness of the ordering/sorting/speed trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing ArrayList and HashMap; forgetting LinkedHashMap or TreeMap and when each fits
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the one-line use case for each and warn that LinkedList.get(i) in a loop is O(n^2)

sections.title: The Core Implementations
sections.content:
The framework ships multiple implementations per interface, each tuned for a different access pattern. For **List**: **ArrayList** (resizable array — O(1) random access via `get`) and **LinkedList** (doubly linked — O(1) insert/remove at the ends, also a `Deque`).

For **Set**: **HashSet** (hash table, unordered, O(1) add/contains), **LinkedHashSet** (preserves insertion order), **TreeSet** (red-black tree, sorted, O(log n)). For **Map**: **HashMap** (hash table, unordered, O(1) average get/put), **LinkedHashMap** (insertion or access order — the basis of LRU caches), **TreeMap** (red-black tree, sorted by key, O(log n), great for range queries). The decision comes down to three questions: do you need **fast lookup**, **insertion order**, or **sorted order**?

emerald|Set|~Unique elements|HashSet: O(1), unordered|LinkedHashSet: insertion order|TreeSet: sorted, O(log n)
amber|Map|~Key to value|HashMap: O(1), unordered|LinkedHashMap: order / LRU|TreeMap: sorted keys, O(log n)

sections.title: Picking the Right Implementation
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only knowing ArrayList and HashMap.** Defaulting to these for everything misses `LinkedList`, `TreeMap`, and `LinkedHashMap` use cases.
- **`LinkedList.get(i)` in a loop.** Random access on a linked list is O(n), so an indexed loop becomes O(n^2). Use `ArrayList` for indexed access.
- **Not knowing LinkedHashMap.** It backs LRU caches via access-order mode and `removeEldestEntry` — a common follow-up.
- **Using TreeSet/TreeMap when order doesn't matter.** You pay O(log n) for sorting you don't need; `HashSet`/`HashMap` are O(1).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ArrayList** — resizable array, O(1) random access; the default List.
- **LinkedList** — doubly linked, O(1) at ends, also a `Deque`; bad for indexed loops.
- **HashSet** — O(1), unordered; **LinkedHashSet** — insertion order; **TreeSet** — sorted, O(log n).
- **HashMap** — O(1), unordered; **LinkedHashMap** — insertion/access order, LRU caches.
- **TreeMap** — sorted by key, O(log n), supports range queries (`headMap`, `tailMap`, `subMap`).
- Choose by three questions: **fast lookup, insertion order, or sorted order**.
- Start with ArrayList / HashSet / HashMap; switch only when the use case demands it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: For List, the two main implementations are ArrayList and LinkedList. ArrayList uses a resizable array internally, so it's great for random access — calling get with an index is constant time. LinkedList uses a doubly linked structure, so it's better when you frequently insert or remove at the beginning or end, and it also implements Deque so you can treat it like a stack or queue. Use ArrayList for indexed access; use LinkedList for queue-like work. For Set you have three choices. HashSet is backed by a hash table, so it's unordered but very fast — add and contains are constant time on average. LinkedHashSet is like HashSet but preserves insertion order. TreeSet uses a red-black tree, so it keeps elements sorted, with log-n operations. Use HashSet for speed, LinkedHashSet when order matters, and TreeSet when you need sorted iteration. For Map it's the same pattern. HashMap is a hash table — unordered, but get and put are constant time on average. LinkedHashMap preserves insertion or access order, which makes it perfect for building an LRU cache. TreeMap is a red-black tree, so keys are sorted and you get range queries like headMap and tailMap, at log-n cost. The way to choose is to ask three questions: do I need fast lookup, insertion order, or sorted order? Two big mistakes to avoid: don't only ever reach for ArrayList and HashMap, and never call get with an index in a loop on a LinkedList, because that's quadratic time. Start with ArrayList, HashSet, and HashMap, then switch to the ordered or sorted variants only when your use case actually needs them.
